opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that you can't optimize what you can't measure. Everyone wants this flywheel where production traffic flows back into training, the model gets better, you redeploy, and it keeps improving on its own. But the very first question is: better at what? If you can't answer that crisply, the loop has nothing to close on.

In a lot of the teams we work with, evaluation is still pretty ad hoc. Someone eyeballs a few outputs, runs a public benchmark that has little to do with their product, and makes a gut call. That's fine for a demo, but it breaks down when you try to automate. An automated loop is just repeated decision-making: should this fine-tuned checkpoint replace the one in production? Is this new data helping or hurting? Did quality regress for some segment of users? Every one of those needs a well-defined, ideally quantitative criterion tied to what the application actually needs to do.

Once you have that, a lot of things snap into place. You can generate or curate training data aimed at the gaps the evals reveal. You can use the evals as a reward signal for reinforcement fine-tuning. You can gate deployments and roll back automatically. And you can make the cost and latency trade-offs explicit, because sometimes a smaller, faster model clears the bar just as well as a big one, and you'd never know without a clear target.

So it's not that evaluation is the glamorous part. It's that it's the foundation. Without it, "closing the loop" is really just retraining and hoping. With it, the system can make good decisions on its own, and that's when you get compounding improvement in quality, speed, and cost.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation criteria are needed to decide whether a fine-tuned checkpoint should replace production and whether new data helps or hurts.

r002.rationale: It says evals can serve as a reward signal for reinforcement fine-tuning, providing feedback about model performance against defined application needs.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify model evaluation as a new skill for application developers who already know product analytics and experimentation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this comes directly out of what we see when we work with teams who are putting models into production. The way I think about it is, the loop between training and inference is essentially a feedback loop, right? You deploy a model, it serves real traffic, that traffic tells you something about where the model is weak, and ideally that signal flows back into the next round of tuning or distillation or whatever you're doing to improve the model. And then the improved model goes back into production. That's the loop.

The question is, what actually drives that loop? If a human has to sit in the middle and look at outputs and say "this one is good, this one is bad," you're never going to close it automatically. It's just too slow and it doesn't scale. So the thing that lets you take the human out of the critical path is having a precise, measurable definition of what "good" means for your product. That's the evaluation criteria.

And I want to emphasize, this is actually the hardest part. People think the hard part is the infrastructure, the fine-tuning pipeline, the serving stack. Those are hard, but they're solvable engineering problems. The really hard part is that most teams, when we first talk to them, cannot tell us in concrete terms what a good response looks like for their application. They have intuitions. They have a few examples. But they don't have a specification that a machine can score against.

Once you have that, everything downstream becomes mechanical. You can take production traffic, run it through your evaluator, identify the failure cases, and those become your training signal, whether that's for supervised fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning with a reward model, or using a bigger model as a teacher. You train a new candidate, you run the same evaluation on it, and if it's better, you promote it. If it's not, you don't. No human needs to make that judgment call, because the judgment has already been encoded in the criteria.

So that's why I say it's the starting point. It's not that evaluation is one step in the pipeline. It's that the evaluation criteria define what the entire pipeline is optimizing toward. Without it you don't have a loop, you have a bunch of disconnected steps with a person manually bridging the gaps. And the teams that figure this out early, that invest in really nailing their evals, those are the ones that end up iterating ten times faster than everyone else, because every improvement cycle just runs on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says to evaluate a new candidate against the same criteria and promote it if it is better, or reject it if it is not.

r002.rationale: It explains that evaluation identifies production failure cases that become a training signal, and that the criteria specify what counts as good. It also names reinforcement learning with a reward model as one possible training approach.

r003.rationale: The response describes defining evaluation criteria as difficult, but does not identify model evaluation as a new skill for application developers familiar with product analytics and experimentation.

astra-6.text:
Because you need to define what “better” means before you can automate improvement. At inference time, you’re seeing how the model behaves on real inputs. But those observations don’t automatically tell you what should go back into training. You need evaluation criteria that connect that behavior to the outcome you actually care about.

Once you have that, you can identify where the model falls short, use those examples to guide training, and evaluate whether the next version actually improves things. Without a clear evaluation signal, you can automate the mechanics of retraining, but you haven’t really closed the loop—you don’t know whether you’re moving in the right direction.

r001.rationale: It says criteria show whether a new version improves, but does not explain evaluating whether switching models improves or degrades performance.

r002.rationale: It describes using evaluation signals to guide training, but does not mention RFT or feedback relative to expectations.

r003.rationale: It does not identify model evaluation as a new skill for developers familiar with product analytics and experimentation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because before you can close the loop automatically, you need to define what a better model actually means for your application. Training loss alone doesn’t tell you whether the model is doing a good job for users. You need evaluation criteria that connect model behavior to the outcome you care about.

Once you have that, inference becomes a source of feedback. You can identify where the model is failing, use those examples to improve the training data, train a new version, and evaluate whether it actually improved. Those criteria also help you decide whether a new model is ready to deploy.

Without that signal, you can automate the mechanics of retraining, but you don’t know whether the loop is making the system better. That’s why I see evaluation as the starting point: it gives the whole process a direction.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation criteria let developers determine whether a new model actually improved, which communicates whether changing models improves performance.

r002.rationale: It describes evaluation feedback in a training loop but does not mention RFT or feedback relative to expectations.

r003.rationale: It does not identify model evaluation as a new skill or refer to developers’ familiarity with product analytics and experimentation.
